b8daf950f514a5a9: NAGOYA: Asian Games organisers admitted on Saturday they were "not satisfied" with ticket sales after swathes of empty seats were seen at the main stadium and other venues in Japan.
The 100m sprints are one of the highlights of any Games, but the 30,000-capacity Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium appeared to be only about one-quarter full on Friday night for the blue-riband events.
Even the prospect of a women's pole vault gold for Japan's Misaki Morota could not pull in the home punters in big numbers at the start of the weekend.
The Aichi-Nagoya Games said that less than 60% of tickets had been snapped up for eight sports, including football, with a similar amount unsold for the closing ceremony in eight days' time.
"We are not satisfied," said Satoshi Murate, secretary-general of the Games organising committee in response to a question from AFP.
"We will keep aiming for full stadiums, keep selling tickets and work to make sure people who have secured seats actually come," Murate said.
He said more than 90% of tickets were sold for the opening ceremony a week ago, but blamed no-shows for large sections of empty seats greeting the parading athletes and lighting of the Games torch.
"Overall, I think sales are strong," he said.
"But it has been pointed out that there are noticeable empty seats at some competitions.
"There are several reasons. First, some sessions include several matches in one day. Everyone focuses on the headline match," he added.
He said tickets that had been given away to Games stakeholders, such as sponsors, were not always used.
"Seats have been allocated, but some people can't come.
"As a result, some competitions do have noticeable empty seats, and we find that regrettable," he said.
Apology for mix-ups
Murate also apologised for mix-ups with accommodation and transport.
Several teams have rounded on the organisers, with Thailand likening it to a "chaotic" game of "musical chairs" and South Korea saying "they deserve a failing grade".
The biggest issue has been a shortage of rooms for the 17,000 participants, a problem compounded by delays at airports and hours-long waits to board a cruise ship acting as a floating hotel.
No traditional athletes' village has been built, as a cost-cutting measure.
Teams have instead been staying in temporary container-style huts, hotels and the Costa Serena cruise ship.
Erratic transport services have seen competitors' buses to training and venues turning up late or, in some cases, not at all.
"There have been mistakes in accommodation and transport, for various reasons," admitted Murate.
"Whatever the cause, AINAGOC (the organising committee) is responsible for providing the service and I sincerely apologise for the mistakes.
"Our staff work every day to identify the causes of each mistake and make sure they don't happen again," Murate said.
d4d7dcb8899f606e: KAJANG, Sept 26 — Madani Mart is opening master licensing applications to companies, investors, and strategic partners with financial and operational capabilities to accelerate its retail network expansion nationwide.

Deputy Domestic Trade and Cost of Living Minister Datuk Dr Fuziah Salleh said each party appointed by Yayasan Madani will have the opportunity to develop and operate up to 100 Madani Mart branches, subject to set terms and standards.

“Currently, priority will be given to three (master licensees). This means if we appoint three, it will enable the opening of around 300 outlets,” she told Bernama after opening the Madani Mart Taman Sutera branch here today.

Fuziah, who is also Yayasan Madani chairman, said the appointment and branch development rights will be awarded in phases based on capability, performance, and compliance with the conditions established by Yayasan Madani.
She said expansion through this model will begin after Yayasan Madani ensures the supply chain and pricing for about 5,000 stock-keeping units (SKUs) offered by Madani Mart remain stable.
Fuziah said Yayasan Madani is negotiating with several commercial and government-owned banks to provide financing facilities up to RM50 million if required.
She added that the master licensing model was introduced to speed expansion. Opportunities to open individual outlets are still offered to ensure more entrepreneurs can join the network.

“We still want to provide opportunities to individual owners. We do not want a situation where only a select few make a profit,” she said, adding that Madani Mart aims to have at least one branch in every state legislative assembly constituency.

Meanwhile, on the opening of Madani Mart Taman Sutera, Fuziah said the third branch introduces a fresh grocery segment, including fish and vegetables, as well as bulk sales for items that do not require specific licences.
The bulk sales facility offers small traders, food operators, and stall owners options to obtain supplies in larger quantities at competitive prices, helping manage operating costs.
To date, Madani Mart operates two locations in Kuantan, Pahang, before opening in Taman Sutera, which marks the network’s first branch in the Klang Valley.

Madani Mart is a strategic partner of the Ministry of Domestic Trade and Cost of Living (KPDN) in executing the Rahmah Madani Sales Programme (PJRM), with every outlet hosting at least one Rahmah Sale per month and providing payment system facilities for the Rahmah Basic Contribution (SARA) programme. — Bernama
7db71001342ef57f: JOHANNESBURG, Sept 26 — South African police today found another body in Ekurhuleni, east of Johannesburg, bringing to 10 the number of women found dead in the municipality over the past two months.
The discovery adds to growing concern over violence against women in a country long plagued by violent crime, while police work to establish whether the killings are connected.
The body was found in the Tembisa township, police said, without providing further details.

“At this stage, we can only confirm the discovery of the body. Crime scene management and all the necessary role players are currently on the scene,” police spokeswoman Brigadier Brenda Muridili said.
Local television station eNCA reported that the semi-naked body was found at a cemetery.
The nine other victims were mostly in their 20s and 30s, with some found stripped of their clothes and showing signs of sexual assault.
The first victim, a 37-year-old woman, was found naked and bound with cable ties on July 15. A suspect was arrested two days later.
Two other suspects, women aged 31 and 38, were arrested in connection with the ninth victim and charged on Monday.
Police have said that case may have stemmed from a relationship-related matter.
Gender-based violence is endemic in South Africa, despite years of government pledges to tackle the problem and the declaration of gender-based violence as a national disaster.
South Africa, a nation of 62 million people, has one of the world’s highest murder rates, with more than 60 killings a day on average. — AFP
ea7afe75adb84c8f: KUALA LUMPUR: Award-winning veteran actress Datuk Fauziah Nawi has described the late Tan Sri L. Krishnan as a towering figure in Malay cinema, saying his contributions helped pave the way for legendary stars such as Tan Sri P. Ramlee and Datuk Mustapha Maarof.

"Without Tan Sri L. Krishnan, we might not have legendary film stars such as Tan Sri P. Ramlee and Datuk Mustapha Maarof," said Fauziah, who never had the opportunity to work directly with the late filmmaker.

Although she never shared a set with him, she heard numerous stories about his impact from senior artistes, including veteran actress Datuk Rosnani Jamil, which gave her a profound appreciation for his legacy.
Fauziah noted that his contribution was so significant that he could rightfully be regarded as the "Father of the Malay film industry."
Her closest personal encounter with him was at his office when she began doing voice-over work in the late 1970s.
"We could say that he started it all. He played the greatest role in the industry," she said, describing his contribution as "humongous".

Her sentiments were echoed by Universiti Teknologi MARA Faculty of Film, Theatre and Animation senior lecturer Ts. Mastura Muhammad, who said L. Krishnan's death marked the loss of one of the few remaining figures who lived through and helped shape the formative years of Malay cinema.
Mastura added that the filmmaker's 104-year life bridged the era of early studio filmmaking and today's modern cinema.

She noted that during the Golden Age, major studios such as Malay Film Productions Ltd. (Shaw Studio) and Cathay-Keris Film Productions Pte. Ltd. relied heavily on Indian directors who helped transfer technical knowledge to local filmmakers and artistes.

"Among them were B.S. Rajhans, K.M. Basker, B.N. Rao, S. Ramanathan and L. Krishnan, whose work helped introduce and adapt cinematic techniques involving storytelling, musical sequences, performance and staging into Malay cinema."

She emphasised that his legacy serves as an important lesson for film students, demonstrating how Malaysian cinema developed through cultural exchange, collaboration, mentorship and the transfer of knowledge across generations.
His passing, she said, should be viewed not merely as the end of an era, but as a reminder of the foundations upon which the country's film industry was built.
L. Krishnan passed away at the age of 104 in Chiang Mai, Thailand, at 2.15pm local time on Thursday due to age-related health complications.
Regarded as a vital pioneer of classic Malay cinema's Golden Era, he was born on Oct 21, 1922, in Madras, India.
He played a pivotal role in nurturing local talent, most notably introducing P. Ramlee to the silver screen through the 1950 film Bakti.
f05a517713007f82: SEREMBAN: Polis telah merekodkan keterangan 21 individu, termasuk pelajar, guru, dan ibu bapa mangsa bagi membantu siasatan berhubung kematian seorang pelajar lelaki di Kuala Pilah, semalam.
Ketua Polis Negeri Sembilan, Alzafny Ahmad, berkata setakat ini punca kematian Muhammad Idlan Fareeq Shahril yang berusia 14 tahun masih belum diperoleh.
"Punca kematian belum dapat ditentukan pada masa ini, dan masih menunggu keputusan ujian lanjutan," katanya kepada pemberita di sini hari ini.
Terdahulu, Alzafny berkata seorang pelajar tingkatan empat direman enam hari bagi membantu siasatan dan kes disiasat mengikut Seksyen 302 Kanun Keseksaan.
Beliau berkata pihaknya telah dimaklumkan mengenai satu kejadian mendatangkan kecederaan terhadap pelajar berusia 14 tahun di sebuah sekolah di Kuala Pilah.
Mangsa telah dibawa ke Hospital Tuanku Ampuan Najihah (HTAN) Kuala Pilah, dan disahkan meninggal dunia.
Siasatan awal mendapati kejadian berlaku kira-kira 8 malam semalam di sebuah asrama sekolah menengah di daerah Kuala Pilah.
152fd51979ccca6d: KUALA LUMPUR: Families of 55 Malaysians still unaccounted for following the Aug 26 glacial flash floods in Nepal will meet Wisma Putra officials tomorrow, seeking answers over the search for their loved ones.

This comes after more than a month of uncertainty, with the families seeking clearer information on what happened at Nepal's Rasuwagadhi-Kerung border area, where some of the missing Malaysians were believed to have been last seen.

Malaysia Solidarity: Families in Hope (MASFIH) spokesman Dr Manivannan Rethinam said the families appreciated the government's efforts, including the deployment of the Special Malaysia Disaster Assistance and Rescue Team (SMART) and diplomatic engagement led by Wisma Putra, but wanted greater clarity over developments on the China-Tibet side as well.

"Our concern is not about the dedication or professionalism of SMART personnel, but whether the operation was carried out at the right time, based on the right priorities and whether the areas identified by the families were thoroughly searched," he told the New Straits Times.

SMART's 11-member team was deployed to Nepal on Sept 5 and conducted ground searches and drone surveillance in areas approved and deemed safe by the Nepalese authorities before returning to Malaysia on Sept 14.
Wisma Putra had said SMART's return did not mean efforts to establish the status of the 55 Malaysians had ended.
The Nepalese authorities will continue the search, verification and identification efforts while Malaysia maintained diplomatic engagement with the relevant authorities.
"Tomorrow's meeting will involve representatives from SMART, police, Chemistry Department, Malaysian Embassy in Kathmandu and National Registration Department (JPN)," he said.
Dr Manivannan is among the next-of-kin whose younger sister, Komathi, 48 is among the 55 Malaysians still missing after the glacier floods in Nepal on Aug 26.
The families are also seeking representation from the Malaysian Embassy in Beijing, Bank Negara Malaysia and the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC) at the meeting tomorrow.

He said the families also wanted the embassy in Beijing to explain Malaysia's engagement with Chinese authorities on search and recovery efforts, identification and last-known-location information, saying this would compliment the technical briefing expected from the Chemistry Department.

"The families are also seeking guidance from Bank Negara Malaysia and the AGC on the financial and legal implications of having a family member remain missing, including matters involving loans, insurance, bank accounts, property, business interests, assets and succession".
Dr Manivannan said the requests were intended to address practical problems faced by families after more than a month of uncertainty.

"This is not an additional demand for the sake of having more agencies at the table. These requests arise from specific information gaps and practical issues that the families are now facing," he said.
The meeting follows the first formal Government engagement with affected families on Day 5 (Aug 30), although not all families were represented then.

It also comes after Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim spoke with Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah on Sept 22 and raised the need for a formal mechanism to assist families should the Malaysians remain unaccounted for.
Anwar had said Shah had assured him that search efforts would continue despite increasingly difficult conditions on the ground.
6f9157aabb078eb3: KUALA LUMPUR: An eighth-place finish in an Asian Games final rarely sounds like cause for celebration, but for national rifle shooter Gan Chen Jie, her outing in the women's 50-metre rifle 3 positions on Saturday delivered both a historic milestone and a sobering reality check.

Competing in her maiden Asian Games final at the Aichi Prefectural General Shooting Gallery, the 21-year-old reigning SEA Games champion found the spotlight unforgiving, carding 299.1 points to become the first shooter eliminated among the eight finalists.
China's Han Jiayu put on a masterclass to capture gold in a Games and Asian record score of 359.0, followed by compatriot Zhang Liyuan (358.8) and South Korea's Kim Jieun (348.4).
Yet, Chen Jie's early exit did little to diminish her landmark achievement on the preliminary range.

For over a decade, Malaysian women had repeatedly hit a brick wall in the 3-positions event, dating back to Guangzhou 2010 when veteran Nur Suryani Taibi missed the final cut by a single spot in ninth.
Subsequent campaigns in Incheon, Jakarta, and Hangzhou all yielded premature exits.

Chen Jie shattered that barrier during morning qualification, amassing 587 points to post the highest individual tally by a Malaysian woman in the discipline at the Asian Games, earning a final berth in the 33-shooter field.

Her efforts also spearheaded Malaysia to a seventh-place finish in the 11-nation team event with a combined 1,746, flanked by Alia Husna Budruddin (583) and Nur Suryani (576) — finishing as the top Southeast Asian nation ahead of Indonesia, Vietnam, and Thailand.

While the day proved Malaysia can now earn a seat at Asia's top table, Chen Jie's elimination also highlighted the psychological gap at this level — a reminder of the unforgiving isolation of the sport.

"When you are on that firing line, nobody else can step in to help. Everything rests entirely on the shooter," said national pistol coach Firdaus Rahim in an assessment he made in the last two days of competition.
All eyes in the national shooting camp now turn to Sunday's action, which represents Malaysia's final opportunity to avoid returning home empty-handed from Aichi.

The contingent will mount its last stand in the women's 25m pistol individual event through two-time Commonwealth Games medallist Alia Sazana Azahari and Nurul Syasya Nadiah Arifin, with Firdaus confirming the squad have regrouped to ensure past finishing lapses are not repeated on the final day of competition.
2e1af766f2e994d8: LONDON: Libya's National Oil Corporation (NOC) said on Saturday it has shut down one of the refining units at the Zawiya refinery due to the continued forced closure of the Sharara crude pipeline valve by armed groups belonging to the Petroleum Facilities Guard.
The corporation warned that ongoing disruptions to the flow of crude could directly impact state oil revenue, increase fuel import costs and harm the national economy.
The closure has reduced cumulative production at the Sharara field by 942,376 barrels over five days through Friday, causing direct financial losses of about US$95 million, the NOC said.
Lost output on Friday alone totalled 222,014 barrels, according to NOC.
60e3e9202dcddce7: KUALA LUMPUR: An AirAsia pilot unknowingly helped fulfil a passenger's desperate hope that her sister would make it back in time to bid their late grandmother a final farewell.

Koh Yew Weng, 37, better known as Eric, was piloting flight AK5135 from Kota Kinabalu to Kuala Lumpur at 6am on Tuesday when a woman posted a plea on social media asking the captain to fly faster so her sister could attend the funeral before the burial.
Eric only discovered the post after landing back in Kota Kinabalu later that day.
"I never expected a coincidence like this could happen. I did not know about the post when we took off.
"I only saw it after landing back in Kota Kinabalu. Only then did I understand what had happened," he said when contacted today.
The flight had faced the possibility of operational delays after drone activity disrupted runway operations at Kota Kinabalu International Airport that morning.
Air traffic control had to operate the airport's single runway in reverse, with one direction used for take-offs and the other for landings.
Eric said he and his co-pilot had initially anticipated significant delays due to the runway constraints.
"However, we were able to push back earlier despite heavy rain at the time. So, despite the runway restrictions, we did not experience long departure delays," he said.
The flight's smooth departure allowed the passenger to arrive in Kuala Lumpur on schedule, as her family had hoped.
"I have been a pilot for 10 years, and while various things have happened throughout that time, this incident stands out as a touching coincidence.
"When we were flying the aircraft, we had no idea someone was desperately hoping the flight would not be delayed," he said.
Eric said he was merely carrying out his duty and was thankful everything went smoothly, particularly after learning that the passenger had made it in time to see her grandmother's remains.
Earlier, Threads user @mierazatie posted a plea addressed to the captain of flight AK5135, hoping the aircraft would arrive promptly so her sister could see their grandmother before the burial.
Hours later, Eric replied to the post, confirming that he was the captain who operated the flight and expressing hope that her sister would make it in time.
The woman later shared that her sister had arrived in time and managed to kiss their grandmother one last time.
7e2df78356fce660: PETALING JAYA: Malaysia perlu memperkukuh pertahanan negara, khasnya di Sabah sebagai langkah berjaga-jaga jika berlaku pertembungan antara kuasa besar di Laut China Selatan.
Menteri Pertahanan, Khaled Nordin, berkata Putrajaya bimbang konflik atau "insiden luar jangka" di kawasan maritim itu boleh merebak ke Malaysia, khasnya Sabah.

“Kalau berlaku perkara tidak dijangka, kita tahu cabaran Laut China Selatan dan persaingan antara kuasa-kuasa besar. Jika berlaku di kawasan itu, yang begitu kecil dari segi geografinya, mungkin menjejaskan negara kita juga,” katanya menurut Bernama selepas pelancaran Literasi Pertahanan Nasional di Kota Kinabalu.

Beliau mengulas kebimbangan rakyat Sabah susulan kerjasama pertahanan Filipina dan Amerika Syarikat yang meningkatkan pembangunan pangkalan tentera, termasuk di Pulau Balabac, Palawan, kira-kira 50km dari Pulau Banggi di Sabah.

Sejak 2014, China menuntut sebahagian besar kawasan di Laut China Selatan, laluan penting bagi perdagangan maritim, perkapalan global dan aktiviti perikanan. Tetapi, tuntutan Beijing itu dipertikaikan beberapa negara termasuk Filipina, Malaysia serta Vietnam.

Menurut Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative, badan pemikir berpangkalan di AS, sekurang-kurangnya sebuah kapal pengawal pantai China memasuki dan beroperasi di perairan Malaysia setiap hari antara 1 Jan hingga 27 Sept 2024.
Khaled mengulangi Malaysia menghormati hak Filipina memperkukuh keupayaan pertahanannya melalui kerjasama dengan Washington.
Tetapi, katanya, pembangunan pangkalan di Pulau Balabac khususnya memerlukan perhatian daripada Putrajaya disebabkan kedudukannya berhampiran Sabah.
“Setiap negara mempunyai hak untuk memperkukuh pertahanan negara masing-masing.
“Itu hak mereka, kita tidak mempertikaikan, tetapi sebagai sebuah negara jiran, kita beri perhatian dan kita wajar mengambil tindakan yang boleh membantu negara kita dari segi pertahanan.”
be4527e4a17844f4: PETALING JAYA: Goh Sze Fei-Nur Izzuddin Rumsani and Pearly Tan-M Thinaah are in the Asian Games badminton quarter-finals after scoring convincing wins over their Japanese and Thai opponents in the last-16 today.
Both pairs are one step away from securing at least a bronze medal, as all semi-finalists are guaranteed a podium finish.
Sze Fei-Izzuddin, ranked world No 6, overcame Japan's ninth-ranked pair, Takuro Hoki-Yugo Kabayashi, 21-19, 21-16 in 35 minutes at the Ichinomiya City Municipal Gymnasium in Aichi, Japan.
The Malaysians will face a tougher test in the quarter-finals tomorrow against China's world No 3 pair, Liang Wei Keng-Wang Chang.
In the women's doubles, world No 5 pair Pearly-Thinaah needed just 29 minutes to dispatch Thailand's Napapakorn Tungkasatan-Hathaithip Mijad 21-8, 21-12.
In the semi-finals tomorrow, they will face India's world No 26 duo Gayatri Gopichand-Treesa Jolly, who shocked Japan's third-ranked pair Yuki Fukushima-Mayu Matsumoto in straight games.
Malaysia won a men's doubles bronze at the last Asian Games in 2022 through Aaron Chia-Soh Wooi Yik.
Vivian Hoo-Woon Khe Wei secured a bronze in the women's doubles at the 2014 games.
18d6bb9203d4ce63: NAGOYA: Keirin specialists Azizulhasni Awang and Shah Firdaus Sahrom will still face tough opposition even if Japan's star rider Kaiya Ota sits out the event at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, says national head coach Harnizam Basri.

The world No. 4 Ota and his teammates Minato Nakaishi (No. 16) and Shinji Nakano (No. 25) are expected to be the main threats to Azizulhasni (No. 13) and Shah Firdaus (No. 67) in both the keirin and individual sprint events.
The track cycling event will run from Sept 29-Oct 2 at the Izu Velodrome in Shizuoka.
Ota is, however, said to be focusing more on the individual sprint event and could skip the keirin.
"We heard the same thing but we do not know if it is actually true," said Harnizam.
"We will not be sure until the start lists are out."
Harnizam, however, stressed that Azizulhasni and Shah will have plenty of other rivals to worry about.
This includes China's Li Zhiwei (No. 15) and Xie Han (No. 20) as well as Thailand's Jai Angsuthasawit - the Asian Games keirin champion from Indonesia 2018 - and Taiwan's Kang Shih-Feng.
"The other two Japanese riders (Nakano, Nakaishi) are also very strong and then we also have the riders from China," said Harnizam.
"China is very hard to anticipate, they have a lot of riders in their system, they might not even send their highest ranked guys.
"And then you have riders such as Jai and Shih-Feng, who have a knack of finding the right wheel to follow."
Harnizam added that the squad, which arrived in Japan from their Brisbane camp two days ago, will begin training at the Izu Velodrome on Sunday.
f068ceffb7836a37: MADRID, Sept 26 — A woman who was allegedly deceived into travelling to Pakistan and forced to marry a cousin has been rescued and returned to Spain, police said on Saturday.
Two men aged 41 and 45 were arrested at Barcelona airport on July 21 on suspicion of human trafficking for the purpose of forced marriage, Catalonia’s regional police said in a statement.

The woman travelled to Pakistan in September 2025 after a relative allegedly told her that her family had dropped its opposition to her relationship with a Pakistani national who owns a computer shop in Barcelona.
Once there, however, relatives allegedly confiscated her Spanish passport, confined her to a family home and arranged her marriage to a cousin despite her opposition.
Her partner reported to police in April that she had been forcibly taken to Pakistan by members of her family.
He had previously been attacked with a bladed weapon in Barcelona by two men allegedly linked to the case.
Spanish police, working with Spain’s embassy in Pakistan, subsequently located the woman and organised her rescue and return to Spain.
She was given specialist support after returning, police said.
The investigation remained open while police worked to identify all those involved in the alleged forced marriage and the attack on her partner.

Barcelona has a sizeable Pakistani community, with more than 26,000 Pakistani nationals registered in the city, making it the third-largest foreign nationality group after Italians and Colombians. — AFP
db10c34340b7ccb0: AICHI: National men's doubles pair Goh Sze Fei-Nur Izzuddin Rumsani kept their dreams of winning a medal at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games alive after advancing to the quarter-finals on Saturday.

Should they succeed in reaching the top four, Sze Fei-Izzuddin will be guaranteed at least a bronze medal for Malaysia.
Meanwhile, national men's singles player Justin Hoh's campaign ended in the third round after losing to former world champion Loh Kean Yew of Singapore.

cb3f4788d0f636b2: NAGOYA: Malaysia's aspiration to add to its gold medal collection at the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Games shone brightly once again as two of the country's squash champions advanced to the final of their respective singles events today.
World No 5 S Sivasangari booked her ticket to the final after defeating Hong Kong’s Chan Sin Yuk 11-6, 11-8, 11-7 in the semi-finals at the Nagoya Kinjofuto Arena.
The victory sees the 27-year-old coming closer to defending the gold medal she won at the Hangzhou 2022 Asian Games.
Sivasangari will face India's Anahat Singh, the world No 17, in the final tomorrow.

However, Sivasangari cannot take the challenge of the 18-year-old player lightly given that the Asian Games championship also offers an automatic slot to the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games.

acf384d16366edfd: KIRTIPUR: Pulled alive 10 days after catastrophic floods trapped him in a tunnel, Nepali hydropower worker Kabir Maharjan is determined to help rebuild his country despite his own harrowing ordeal.
Traditional music and tearful relatives welcomed the 45-year-old when he returned home on Friday after spending weeks recovering at a hospital in Kathmandu.
"Life is precious. Hundreds of people have died but I survived," the father of two told AFP, his voice choked with emotion.
"Perhaps I still have work to do for my society, for the country, and my home and family," he added.
The Aug 26 flood, triggered by a glacial mountain collapse near the China-Nepal border, has killed more than 1,400 people, the majority in Nepal.
Over 5,000 remain missing in Nepal since the tsunami-like waves swept away roads, bridges and settlements in the mountainous regions up north, and battered crucial hydropower projects.
Maharjan, who was among hundreds of workers employed at projects hit by the floods, was eventually airlifted from the worst-hit Rasuwa region.
His miraculous rescue on Sept 4, alongside fellow worker Sanjay Sah, offered a rare moment of hope during the disaster.
Now, as Nepal shifts from emergency response to reconstruction, he said he hopes to return to his profession.
"There is risk in everything, but still we have to win over it," he said.
'Work is our karma'
More than 800 people employed at hydropower projects in Nepal remain unaccounted for, the energy minister told parliament last week.
Forty-seven bodies have been recovered from flood-hit project sites, while rescue teams continue to comb through the ruins.
Maharjan said he survived by reaching an upper floor of the tunnel site and drinking water while waiting for help.
"Whenever I was awake, I would try to find a way out," he said.
Days later, he saw what appeared to be a light and heard voices.
"I thought I imagined it. But I called out, and they answered," he said.
For Maharjan, the country's long road to recovery mirrors his own - he is still recovering from wounds on his hand and leg.
However, he said the rebuilding efforts could also provide spiritual sustenance.
"While we are alive, we must be patient and do our work," he said.
"Work is our karma," he added.
Continuing crisis
The flooding dealt a major blow to Nepal's hydropower generation system, which is central to the country's development ambitions and export earnings.
The government estimates overall reconstruction could cost US$4.8 billion, with thousands of people displaced and key infrastructure damaged.
The disaster has also renewed scrutiny of how roads, hydropower plants and trade corridors are built in Nepal's challenging mountain terrain.

Prime minister Balendra Shah told the UN on Thursday that the flooding was "a warning to the world" about the growing dangers posed by climate change, urging greater international support to help Nepal adapt and rebuild.
Aid groups have warned that the humanitarian crisis is far from over.

"The floodwaters may have receded, but for thousands of people, the crisis is far from over," David Fisher, head of delegation for the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies in Nepal, said Friday.
"It is urgent to take the next steps in the recovery process to keep people healthy and avoid a spiral into poverty," he said.
1e40ef1f1b0c77cd: PAPAR: A new RM18.23 million hostel complex at SMK Majakir here has been completed, increasing the school's accommodation capacity from 160 to 300 students.
Papar member of parliament Datuk Armizan Ali said the project, completed on April 30, was handed over by the Sabah Education Department (JPNS) to the Papar District Education Office (PPD) today.
He said the project was particularly important for students living far from the school who depended on hostel accommodation as daily commuting was difficult.
"The old hostel could only accommodate 160 students, comprising 80 boys and 80 girls.
"However, the building was originally designed as classrooms and administrative facilities before being converted into a hostel to meet students' accommodation needs," he said in a statement today.
The new complex comprises two two-storey hostel blocks, warden houses, dormitories for students with disabilities, common rooms, isolation rooms, warden offices and reception rooms.
It also includes two sports courts, a hostel supervisor's office and a dining hall that can accommodate up to 300 people.
Armizan said the old hostel would be considered for conversion back into classrooms, providing the school with additional learning space.
ea6ebb5fcae00620: HAMILTON: TikTok bersetuju membayar USD116 juta bagi menyelesaikan saman difailkan Alabama berhubung dakwaan platform itu memudaratkan pengguna muda menerusi reka bentuk yang mendorong penggunaan secara berlebihan, lapor Anadolu Ajansi memetik media tempatan pada Jumaat.
Menurut Alabama Reflector, penyelesaian itu dicapai antara TikTok dan Peguam Negara Alabama menerusi dekri persetujuan yang dikeluarkan seorang hakim Mahkamah Circuit Montgomery.

Selain bayaran USD116 juta sebagai pampasan, TikTok turut dikehendaki mewujudkan dana berasingan bernilai USD183 juta, bergantung kepada sama ada negeri-negeri lain turut menyertai perjanjian seumpama itu.
Di bawah penyelesaian berkenaan, TikTok perlu menyekat akses pengguna remaja antara tengah malam hingga 6 pagi dan menetapkan had penggunaan harian secara lalai kepada dua jam.
Platform itu juga perlu menyediakan kemudahan kepada ibu bapa untuk memantau serta mengehadkan penggunaan akaun anak-anak mereka.
TikTok bagaimanapun tidak mengakui sebarang salah laku.
Alabama menyaman syarikat itu pada April 2025 dengan mendakwa algoritma TikTok mendedahkan kanak-kanak kepada kandungan berbahaya berkaitan dadah, perbuatan mencederakan diri dan gangguan pemakanan.
Saman itu turut mendakwa reka bentuk platform berkenaan menyebabkan pengguna muda terus menggunakan aplikasi itu bagi menyokong model pengiklanannya.

TikTok sebelum ini memohon supaya saman berkenaan ditolak dengan berhujah bahawa platform dalam talian dilindungi oleh kekebalan undang-undang, selain membangkitkan isu berkaitan undang-undang privasi.

Peguam Negara Alabama Steve Marshall menyifatkan penyelesaian itu sebagai 'hari yang baik' untuk keluarga kerana TikTok kini perlu memberikan kawalan lebih besar kepada ibu bapa terhadap penggunaan aplikasi oleh anak-anak mereka.
TikTok pula berkata keputusan itu selaras dengan komitmen syarikat untuk terus memperkukuh ciri keselamatan bagi melindungi pengguna muda.
7c3e37a07f0dcb97: PETALING JAYA: Malaysia is looking to strengthen its national defence, especially in Sabah, as a precautionary measure in the event of a clash between major powers in the South China Sea.
Defence minister Khaled Nordin said Putrajaya's main concern was that a conflict or "unexpected incident" in the maritime region could spill over to Malaysia, particularly Sabah.

"We know the challenges in the South China Sea and the rivalry between major powers. If something happens in that geographically small area, it could also affect our country,” he said, according to Bernama.
The Philippines and the US have ramped up their defence cooperation in the South China Sea in view of China's actions in the disputed maritime area.
This has led to a buildup of military bases in the Philippines, including one on Balabac island in Palawan, which is about 50km from Sabah's Banggi island.

Since 2014, China has claimed a wide swathe of the South China Sea, a critical channel for maritime trade, global shipping, and fishing, but the Philippines, Malaysia and Vietnam have disputed Beijing's claims.
According to Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative, a US think tank, at least one Chinese coast guard vessel entered and operated in Malaysian waters every day between Jan 1 and Sept 27, 2024.
Khaled maintained that Malaysia respected the right of the Philippines to strengthen its defence capabilities in partnership with Washington.
Nonetheless, he said, the development of the Balabac island base in particular demanded attention from Putrajaya given its proximity to Sabah.
“Every country has its own right to strengthen its national defence.

“That is their right, and we do not dispute it, but as a neighbouring country, we are paying attention (to the development) and should take measures that can help our country in terms of defence," he said.
b5be0a7e66ee0499: SINGAPORE, Sept 26 — Singapore’s government is reviewing property purchases made by officers involved in rail planning after a research paper found public servants appeared more likely than others to buy homes near future MRT stations before the locations were publicly announced.

The Public Service Division (PSD) said the review would cover purchases made between 2007 and 2011, the period highlighted in the paper, involving properties close to locations that were later announced as MRT stations, Singapore-based news outlet CNA reported today.

But the research, published earlier this month by the US-based National Bureau of Economic Research, has not been peer-reviewed and does not establish that individual civil servants committed misconduct.

The researchers said they found a higher incidence of property purchases near planned MRT stations by civil servants than by a comparable group, with the difference concentrated in the one to two years before station locations were publicly announced.

PSD said the statistical patterns were concerning, but did not by themselves establish whether any officer had access to non-public information about MRT station locations or whether such information influenced a property purchase.
“For example, information or speculation about planned MRT lines and stations may already be in the public domain or used to market new property developments,” PSD was quoted as saying last Friday.
The division said it would retrieve available records and examine the circumstances of individual transactions, noting that the purchases took place many years ago.
“If we find evidence that an officer used non-public information to make a property purchase for personal benefit, the case will be referred to the police for further investigation,” PSD said.

The paper estimated that, compared with its control group, civil servants made about 50 additional purchases of properties near future MRT stations two years before announcements and 63 additional purchases one year before.

The researchers put the gross value of those excess pre-announcement purchases at about S$138 million (RM431 million) and said the pattern was concentrated among mid-level officials and those working in agencies involved in MRT planning.

The study also reported similar patterns among people connected to the officials through shared residential addresses, although it used the term “relatives” for convenience and said this did not necessarily mean the individuals were family members.

PSD said Singapore’s public service has long had safeguards against officials using non-public information for personal benefit, including requirements to declare property purchases and controls over access to sensitive information.

It said the safeguards had been strengthened over time, with officers today required to declare and obtain approval before making personal transactions that could be affected by non-public information, including property, vehicles or financial instruments.

The paper, titled ‘Do Social Norms Substitute for Enforcement? Evidence from Public Officials’ Home Purchases in Singapore’, was authored by academics from Columbia University, Stanford University and the University of Hong Kong.

PSD said it had previously announced on September 14 that it was reviewing the paper’s data and methodology and would refer matters to the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau if there was a material basis to do so.
Some Singapore academics acknowledged in the paper have since asked to have their names removed from the acknowledgements, according to local media reports.
PSD said conclusions of wrongdoing must ultimately be based on evidence and the facts of each case.
21812e64b2dd11b3: KUCHING, Sept 26 — A passenger van was impaled by a roadside guardrail after crashing at a traffic light junction in Bandar Baru Samariang this morning.
See Hua Daily News reported that the incident occurred at about 7am today.
The van is believed to have lost control before crashing into the roadside barrier, causing the guardrail to pierce through the vehicle.
The van was carrying one female passenger at the time.
She sustained injuries in the incident and received initial treatment from paramedics at the scene before being taken to Sarawak General Hospital for further treatment. — The Borneo Post
6e34eb69e7f7b5dc: SHAH ALAM, Sept 26 — Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim today questioned the federal Opposition’s priorities, taking a swipe at its MPs for scrutinising his refusal to draw a prime ministerial salary while, he said, saying little about those who “sakau”, or steal, large sums of money.
Anwar recalled being questioned by Opposition MPs in Parliament over how he could support himself without taking his salary as prime minister.
He said he had also been told by the Opposition that even Prophet Muhammad received wages, but added that he had never heard that the Prophet took a salary.

“Then I said, I don’t take a salary, but I don’t fall under the B40 category. Firstly, I take the allowance,” he said during a gathering with Universiti Teknologi MARA (UiTM) alumni and students at the university’s Dewan Agung Tuanku Canselor.
Anwar said the government also provides the vehicle he uses, accommodation at the prime minister’s official residence, Seri Perdana, and flights.
“It’s enough lah. Not rich, but not poor,” he said of his financial position.
He then questioned what the Opposition had chosen to focus on.
“But they want to ‘sibuk’ [interfere], want to be angry. Don’t take a salary, they’re angry. Those who ‘sakau’ [steal] a lot, they don’t mention,” he said, drawing laughter from the audience.
Anwar did not elaborate on whom he was referring to in his remarks about the Opposition.

Last month, Anwar also used the word “sakau” when speaking about alleged past financial mismanagement at Lembaga Tabung Haji (TH), following the government’s July 29 release of a Royal Commission of Inquiry report into the pilgrims’ fund.

The RCI examined TH’s management and operations from 2014 to 2020. The government subsequently said investigations based on the report’s findings would proceed and that action would be taken if breaches of the law were established.
In 2024, PAS president Tan Sri Abdul Hadi Awang reportedly suggested in the Dewan Rakyat that Anwar was seeking to appear more pious than Prophet Muhammad by refusing to accept a salary.
Anwar has declined to draw his salaries as prime minister and finance minister since taking office in November 2022, while continuing to receive his allowance as Tambun MP.
‘I’m not poor’: Accused of acting holier than Prophet for refusing wages, PM Anwar says he’s still earning Parliament allowance
f085a9ccec195db5: KOTA KINABALU, Sept 26 — Parti Bersatu Sabah (PBS) president Datuk Seri Dr Joachim Gunsalam wants the party to be strengthened as a modern, multiracial and integrity-driven entity that remains relevant, while reaffirming its commitment to continue working with Gabungan Rakyat Sabah (GRS).

He said the direction of the new PBS leadership would be based on three main pillars — unity, stability and integrity — in line with the theme of the 41st PBS Congress held today, ‘Unity, Stability, Integrity’.

“We may have different views and approaches, but our goal remains the same: to strengthen PBS and fight for Sabah’s future,” he said when delivering his presidential policy speech at the congress here.
He said the struggle concerning the Malaysia Agreement 1963 (MA63) was not yet over and PBS would continue to play an active role in defending Sabah’s rights and interests.

“This means our struggle is still a long one. PBS will continue to be an active, relevant and consistent voice in defending Sabah’s rights and interests. We do not want MA63 to merely become a political slogan; we want tangible implementation and results that the people can feel,” he said.
On unity, Dr Joachim said PBS needed to continue serving as a political home that united Sabahans regardless of race, religion, district or background.

He said the party would strengthen public participation by increasing the participation of Malays and Muslim Bumiputera, regaining the confidence of the Chinese community and providing greater opportunities for professionals, women and the younger generation.
“PBS does not belong to one race. PBS belongs to everyone who believes in the struggle for Sabah,” he said.
On GRS, he said PBS would continue to be a loyal, constructive and principled partner in the coalition.

Dr Joachim said PBS’ loyalty to the coalition did not mean that the party would lose its identity, but would continue to voice Sabah’s interests, including MA63, rural development, education, the economy, employment opportunities and the people’s well-being.

“We are with GRS, but we remain PBS. In terms of integrity, positions in PBS are not a gift but a trust that requires leaders to work, go to the ground, listen to the people’s problems and seek solutions,” he said. — Bernama
876d1ed843c00fa5: JAKARTA: Wildfires that tore through Indonesian Borneo's vast tropical forests have piled pressure on critically endangered Bornean orangutans, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) said Saturday.
Indonesia has been battling fires for weeks in parts of Borneo and Sumatra, sending suffocating haze across the islands and neighbouring Malaysia and Singapore.
"Fires are currently burning within habitats containing 52% of Borneo's orangutan population, including 13 of the 20 largest remaining populations," it said.
"Fire and smoke exposure impose measurable physiological, behavioural and ecological costs on orangutans in peat forest habitats," the conservation network said.
"During haze, orangutans show signs of fat breakdown despite eating more and resting more, suggesting elevated energy demands likely from an immune system forced to work harder," it said.
"Wildfires have also been reported in the habitats of five gibbon species across Sumatra and Borneo," the conservation network said.

"Gibbons breathe the same smoke-laden air as the people living alongside them, and there is every reason to expect they suffer similar respiratory harm, on top of habitat loss and disruption to the behaviours that keep wild populations viable," it said.
"As of Tuesday, Indonesia had rescued 100 animals, including 53 orangutans, that were threatened by the blazes," a forestry ministry spokesman said.
Conservationists call on the authorities to go beyond first response and implement prevention measures.
"Emergency response must be followed by sustained investment in preventing future fires," Ronna Saab of Forum Konservasi Orangutan Indonesia (FORINA) said in a statement.

Those measures include "protecting and rewetting peatlands, addressing drainage and deforestation, and ensuring burned forests are protected from subsequent conversion and appropriately restored," Ronna said.
The Indonesian government said more than 202,000 hectares of land were burnt countrywide between January and July, the latest available data.
The Nusantara Atlas project has put the number at closer to 900,000 hectares between January and August.
1e641e6e91efe21b: MILAN, Sept 26 — Milan’s main international airport was officially renamed on Friday after former Italian prime minister Silvio Berlusconi, who died in 2023.
The airport is now called Aeroporto Milano-Malpensa Silvio Berlusconi, after the new name was approved in 2024 but faced legal challenges, German news agency dpa reported.

“Knowing that Milan-Malpensa Silvio Berlusconi Airport will welcome thousands of travellers from all over the world every day fills me with pride and emotion,” said Maria Elvira “Marina” Berlusconi, the late politician’s eldest daughter.
The airport is the second largest in Italy after Rome-Fiumicino.
Milan Mayor Giuseppe Sala stayed away from the renaming ceremony in protest, having previously opposed naming the airport after Berlusconi, who was born in the city.
“What was I supposed to do? Turn up with a forced smile?” he commented on Instagram.
Berlusconi was a deeply controversial figure both in Italy and abroad.
He served four terms as prime minister between 1994 and 2011, spending more than nine years in office — longer than any other Italian prime minister since the end of World War II.

His political career was marked by numerous legal fights, including a 2013 conviction for tax fraud and a trial over the so-called “bunga bunga” affair involving parties attended by some underage girls.
He was ultimately acquitted in that case.
Berlusconi’s Forza Italia party is now part of the three-party right-wing coalition led by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy, which has governed Italy since 2022. — Bernama-dpa
69d26d290ee9b50f: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 26 — A post-mortem has failed to establish the cause of death of a 14-year-old boy whose death is being investigated following allegations of bullying at a school hostel in Kuala Pilah, with police awaiting the results of further tests.

Negeri Sembilan police chief Datuk Alzafny Ahmad said the examination was carried out at the Forensic Medicine Department of Tuanku Jaafar Hospital in Seremban from 10.30am today, Harian Metro reported.
“The post-mortem, conducted by HTJ forensic pathologist Dr Akma Nurain Fairuz Mahamad Arif, was completed at 3pm today.
“The results of the post-mortem showed that the cause of death could not be determined at this time, and we are still awaiting the results of further tests,” Alzafny was quoted as saying.
He said police had so far recorded statements from 21 people, including students, teachers and the boy’s parents, as part of the investigation.
The student was found unconscious at the school hostel last night and was taken to Tuanku Ampuan Najihah Hospital in Kuala Pilah, where he was pronounced dead.
Police subsequently detained a 16-year-old student to assist in the investigation and opened an investigation paper under Section 302 of the Penal Code.
The teenager was today remanded for six days, until October 1, to assist police with the investigation.
The Education Ministry has also ordered an immediate audit of the school following the boy’s death and said it would cooperate fully with police.
4db53884b945efd5: Aminata Seck’s detention shows the bargain facing international college athletes: universities eagerly recruit them, but support can disappear when their immigration status becomes precarious Earlier this week, news broke for the first time that Senegalese Division II Kentucky State women’s basketball player Aminata Seck was abducted by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) at Louisville’s Muhammad Ali International Airport on 7 August during a trip to attend the HBCU All-Star game in New York. Seck is listed as a Kentucky State senior and last year started 20 of 26 games, earning third-team all-conference honors and an SIAC Elite 16 award for academic achievement. According to a lawyer involved with her case, Sadiqa Reynolds, Seck has been moved through four different ICE facilities since her initial apprehension: Clay County, Chicago, Clark County and Grayson County. Reynolds noted that the reason for Seck’s imprisonment was a missed student visa deadline – what she characterized as “a paperwork situation” – due to back surgery. Reynolds also said that Seck has been suffering from an ACL injury while detained and has received only ibuprofen but no proper medical care. ICE arrests in Kentucky have risen by 70% this year. Nathan Kalman-Lamb is Associate Professor of Sociology at the University of New Brunswick and co-host of The End of Sport podcast. Simran Kaur Sethi is Assistant Professor of Sport Leadership at the University of Kentucky where she studies equity and inclusion for international college athletes. Derek Silva is Professor of Sociology and Criminology at King’s University College at Western University and co-host of The End of Sport podcast. Continue reading...

8535e2793cc4d7a1: Do we really want a slick digital message board overseen by Amazon? It’s the neighbourhood nonsense we treasure Ring, the Amazon subsidiary of camera-enabled doorbells fame, wants to be an even bigger part of your neighbourhood. Next month in the UK, it will be launching Neighbours, a community app that seeks to replace the now traditional neighbourhood Facebook or WhatsApp group. My first thought was that this is curtain-twitching culture gone mad. If you must have a Ring doorbell (and my instinctive feeling as someone without one, a feeling I will no doubt have until I get one and decide it’s great, is that it’s narc-coded behaviour) then: OK. But does Amazon need to be in charge of a digital village messageboard too? Imogen West-Knights is a writer and journalist Continue reading...
e868635adff68b10: NAGOYA, Sept 26 — China’s 17-year-old sprinter Chen Yujie said she has “no limits” after dominating the women’s 100m final to win Asian Games gold.
Chen stormed to victory in a Games-record 11.06 seconds in Nagoya to showcase her potential.
Chen, who turns 18 in December, called Friday’s emphatic victory “the best present for my birthday”.
But the teenager does not want to stop there.
“Now I am the champion of the Asian Games and I want to achieve more on the international stage, at the world championships and at the Olympics,” she said.
“Now that I have become a champion, my goal will be to defend my title in the future.
“I am now in the position of challenging someone else, instead of waiting to be challenged by others.”
Chen, who will also race in the 200m at the Games, added: “I have no limits.”
Chinese media on Saturday hailed what it hopes will be a new era for Chinese sprinting, having never won 100m or 200m Olympic gold.
The official Olympics website proclaimed her a “new sprint star”.
“I want to leave my mark for the Chinese women’s sprinters and for the Asian sprinters,” said Chen.
Despite the victory, Chen admitted she had been nervous before the final.
“When I was on the training track my legs were shaking,” said the teenager, who beat two-time Olympian Shanti Pereira of Singapore into second by 0.15 seconds.
“I was very scared that this could lead to a false start. I thought a lot about that.”
Chen also defeated the 30-year-old Pereira to win the 200m at the 2025 Asian Athletics Championships. — AFP
909bc973de0583f5: NAGOYA, Sept 26 — Asian Games organisers admitted on Saturday they were “not satisfied” with ticket sales after swathes of empty seats were seen at the main stadium and other venues in Japan.
The 100m sprints are one of the highlights of any Games, but the 30,000-capacity Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium appeared to be only about one-quarter full on Friday night for the blue-riband events.
Even the prospect of a women’s pole vault gold for Japan’s Misaki Morota could not pull in the home punters in big numbers at the start of the weekend.
The Aichi-Nagoya Games said that less than 60 per cent of tickets had been snapped up for eight sports, including football, with a similar amount unsold for the closing ceremony in eight days’ time.
“We are not satisfied,” said Satoshi Murate, secretary-general of the Games organising committee, in response to a question from AFP.
“We will keep aiming for full stadiums, keep selling tickets and work to make sure people who have secured seats actually come.”

He said more than 90 per cent of tickets were sold for the opening ceremony a week ago, but blamed no-shows for large sections of empty seats greeting the parading athletes and lighting of the Games torch.
“Overall I think sales are strong,” he said.
“But it has been pointed out that there are noticeable empty seats at some competitions.
“There are several reasons. First, some sessions include several matches in one day. Everyone focuses on the headline match.”
He said tickets that had been given away to Games stakeholders, such as sponsors, were not always used.
“Seats have been allocated but some people can’t come.
“As a result, some competitions do have noticeable empty seats, and we find that regrettable.”
Apology for mix-ups
Murate also apologised for mix-ups with accommodation and transport.

1e588486cc3e4e18: A tired, simplistic narrative dominates Malaysian campaign stages and social media feeds: that Malay disunity is entirely DAP's fault.

While this rhetoric is highly effective at mobilising voters through fear, it is built on a shallow foundation. Blaming DAP is a convenient distraction, one that deliberately obscures the true root causes of the Malay political crisis.

The reality is that polarisation within the Malay community is not driven by an external threat. It is the direct result of internal dynamics, clashing egos and socioeconomic evolution. DAP did not fracture Malay politics; it has merely been weaponised as a bogeyman whenever the community's internal consensus begins to splinter.

Historically, every major rupture within the Malay political establishment has originated from internal power struggles, not external interference. The historic 1987 Umno crisis — a fierce showdown between Dr Mahathir Mohamad and Tengku Razaleigh Hamzah — birthed Semangat 46.
The 1998 Reformasi movement, sparked by Anwar Ibrahim's sacking from government, led to the creation of PKR. Decades later, the 1MDB scandal triggered the 2016 split that formed Bersatu.

All of these political earthquakes occurred deep within Umno's own backyard. They were driven by leadership conflicts and raw ambition, long before DAP was ever accepted into mainstream ruling coalitions.

Furthermore, the Malay electorate is not, and has never been, a monolith. Even before independence, Malay political thought was fractured into distinct ideological factions. Malay nationalism, anchored by Umno, focused on ethnic privileges and the social contract.
Conversely, Islamic politics, championed by PAS, demanded a state rooted in religious law — a doctrinal divergence that triggered their split from Umno as early as 1951.

Today, progressive movements like PKR and Amanah contest this space by championing institutional reform and social justice within a pluralistic framework, alongside a constantly shifting constellation of splinter parties.

With segments of the electorate prioritising economic integrity, others focusing on religious identity, and some remaining loyal to traditional structures, a fragmented political landscape is inevitable.
Where, then, does DAP fit into this theatre?

The party has become a convenient rhetorical shield. When multiple Malay-based parties are forced to fish from the exact same voter pool, they inevitably fall into a hyper-nationalistic contest to prove who is "more Malay" or "more Islamic".

In this arena, the fastest way to destroy an opponent’s credibility is to label them a "puppet" or "agent" of DAP. This strategy shifts the focus away from a party's own policy failures by exploiting historical trauma and racial anxieties for short-term electoral gain.
Ultimately, a diversification of political choices is a hallmark of a maturing democracy, not a crisis to be feared. It is time for Malay political leaders to stop pointing fingers outwardly.

Blaming DAP will not reunite the community. The real challenge lies in the leadership’s inability to forge a consensus, manage ideological differences with maturity, and prioritise national stability over personal agendas.
Until they look in the mirror, they will continue fighting external shadows.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

92373c2d48160be1: In late August, US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent declared an “economic D-Day” against Iran, promising “the single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled against an adversary”.
The D-Day analogy is an odd one for a campaign whose success ultimately depends on China, an American ally at Normandy but a strategic rival today.

For the Trump administration’s “zero-leakage” policy to succeed, foreign financial institutions would need to monitor and police their own customers. And there is no way to achieve the “total isolation” of the Iranian regime without Chinese banks doing much of the hard work of sanctions enforcement.

Before the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the US Treasury estimated that China purchased roughly 90% of Iran’s oil exports. Years of sanctions have already pushed much of the Iranian oil trade into an alternative system capable of operating without the dollar, the SWIFT interbank payments platform, and the correspondent banks that have long given the US its financial leverage.

Much of this trade moves through Iran’s rahbar shadow-banking system, which according to the Treasury processes “tens of billions of dollars” worth of trade each year, “much of it derived from Iran’s overseas sales of oil and petrochemicals”. Today, Iran settles those sales primarily in renminbi.

Secondary US sanctions have previously changed the behaviour of major Chinese banks even when China officially rejected them. Within the first week of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, for example, the offshore units of the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) stopped issuing dollar-denominated letters of credit for purchases of physical Russian commodities.

Renminbi-denominated credit lines remained available for some customers but required senior management approval. The Bank of China (BOC) restricted financing for Russian commodities, while its Singapore branch went even further and ceased financing transactions involving Russian companies and oil.
America’s sanctions blind spot

But China’s largest banks—its policy banks and the “big four” state-owned commercial banks, the ICBC, the BOC, the China Construction Bank, and the Agricultural Bank of China—are not America’s hardest enforcement problem.
Their global operations require them to maintain access to dollar liquidity and correspondent banking relationships, which are far more valuable than any business with sanctioned Iranian entities.

This dependence on the global dollar system gives them powerful incentives to limit their exposure to US sanctions. As former Treasury secretary Janet L Yellen observed, China’s large banks “are not banks that we most need to worry about” as they “really, really value their correspondent-banking relations”.

The greater challenge lies deeper within the Chinese financial system, among thousands of smaller regional banks with far less exposure to the dollar-based system and therefore with less to lose if that access is cut off.
In 2023, the People’s Bank of China counted more than 3,800 urban and rural banks and credit cooperatives, in addition to private banks and other institutions.
In 2024, as the US threatened Chinese banks with secondary sanctions, Russian companies increasingly turned to smaller regional institutions with minimal ties to Western markets.

The real question facing the Trump administration is whether it can compel or induce smaller Chinese banks to scrutinise customers and transactions deliberately structured to conceal Iranian connections—and refuse the business once they uncover them.

Iran’s rahbars use foreign-exchange houses, layers of offshore shell companies, and bank accounts in the United Arab Emirates, Hong Kong, and Singapore to move oil proceeds on behalf of sanctioned Iranian entities.
Chinese buyers of Iranian crude, especially independent “teapot” refiners in Shandong, which have absorbed most of the sanctioned oil, do not need to send money to an Iranian bank.
A buyer can simply pay an offshore front company in renminbi. The money can then be used to pay Chinese suppliers on Iran’s behalf or sent elsewhere.
On paper, the transaction may have no connection to Iran. To the Chinese bank processing the payment, it could look like an ordinary transfer from a Hong Kong trading firm to a company in Dubai.

Internal records from the Iranian exchange house Radin, for example, identified dozens of China-based front companies maintaining accounts at Chinese banks. FinCEN has similarly documented transactions operated by Hong Kong-based shell companies that it linked to Iran’s shadow-banking network.

This makes compliance much harder. Instead of simply refusing to do business with sanctioned entities, banks now have to uncover hidden links to Iran in accounts and transactions where no Iranian name appears at all. That requires more than routine customer onboarding and sanctions-list screening.

Banks must scrutinise beneficial ownership and counterparties more closely and examine the purpose of payments, while anti-money laundering teams must devote resources to reviewing transaction documentation and looking for payment patterns indicating that seemingly ordinary transactions may actually be moving money for sanctioned Iranian entities.

The US Treasury is now explicitly pushing this investigative burden onto foreign banks. In April, the Office of Foreign Assets Control urged financial institutions to subject independent teapot oil refineries in China to enhanced due diligence and warned that the US government is prepared to use secondary sanctions against them.
The Treasury has since made clear that its latest sanctions campaign, Operation Economic Outcast, could include cutting foreign banks off from the dollar-based system.
The compliance trap

In principle, Chinese law already requires banks to conduct “know your customer” verification and maintain financial-crime controls. In 2022, the Financial Action Task Force rated China’s anti-money laundering regime as “largely compliant” with its due-diligence standards.

China has implemented additional measures since then. Its revised anti-money laundering law, which took effect in January 2025, requires financial institutions to verify customers and beneficial owners, understand the nature of business relationships, and, in certain high-risk cases, investigate the source of funds and the purpose of transactions.

Banks must also monitor customers and transactions and investigate activity that departs from established patterns. More detailed rules implemented in January 2026 allow banks to refuse transactions or terminate relationships when they cannot adequately resolve money-laundering concerns.

But anti-money laundering compliance and US sanctions enforcement are not the same thing. Finding an Iranian connection may prompt a Chinese bank to look more closely at a transaction if there are signs of money laundering. It does not, however, mean that under Chinese law they must reject it just because the US has sanctioned one of the parties.

In some cases, Chinese regulations pull banks in the opposite direction. In May, the Chinese ministry of commerce (Mofcom) issued a blocking order covering five independent Chinese refiners sanctioned by the US for purchasing Iranian oil. Four are smaller regional teapot refiners.

The fifth, Hengli Petrochemical’s Dalian refinery, can process 400,000 barrels a day and belongs to the Hengli Group, a Fortune 500 company. It is the largest Chinese refiner sanctioned by the US so far.

Mofcom’s order states that US sanctions against these five refiners “must not be recognised, implemented, or complied with”. Violations of the order can result in administrative penalties and expose banks and other companies to claims for damages in Chinese courts.

A Chinese bank can still refuse to process a transaction because of money-laundering concerns or other compliance risks, but it cannot refuse a transaction or sever a relationship specifically to comply with the covered US sanctions without violating the order.
As the US extends secondary sanctions to cover more economically and politically significant Chinese entities, such blocking orders are likely to become more common.
China now has a sophisticated legal and administrative apparatus that can make the extraterritorial application of US sanctions increasingly difficult—or, in some cases, moot.

This exposes a structural constraint on US sanctions power. Large state-owned Chinese banks have too much to lose if they are cut off from the dollar system. But US leverage weakens as transactions move to smaller banks with fewer ties to the US and Western financial markets.

The US government is thus left in the awkward position of asking Chinese banks to uncover hidden ties to sanctioned entities in Iran (or North Korea and Russia) and then act on those findings, even when that could put them at odds with Chinese law.

Chinese banks are certainly willing to carry out the anti-money laundering checks required by Chinese regulations, but they have little incentive to go looking for links to sanctioned entities when discovering them could create new legal problems.

In such circumstances, knowing less and maintaining plausible deniability is institutionally safer than knowing more. And unless Chinese banks closely police their own clients as payment networks adapt, sanctions will remain porous, with payments migrating to new shell companies and intermediaries.
China’s new bargaining chip

Despite having the tools to retaliate against new US sanctions, China has used them selectively. Since President Donald Trump restored “maximum pressure” on Iran in February 2025, US sanctions against Chinese entities have mostly targeted specific shadow-fleet vessels, independent refineries in Shandong Province, and shipping terminal operators (Hengli Petrochemical’s Dalian refinery, the only large integrated Chinese independent refiner sanctioned so far, remains the notable exception).
China’s response has consisted mostly of formulaic foreign ministry statements rejecting the unilateral nature of US sanctions and pledging to protect Chinese companies and citizens.

Mofcom’s May 2 blocking order remains the only consequential countermeasure, and it is narrow and targeted. Yet only days after it was issued, Chinese financial regulators reportedly instructed major Chinese banks to suspend new renminbi lending to the five sanctioned refiners while leaving existing credit lines in place.
These actions are not necessarily contradictory. China can reject the extraterritorial application of US sanctions while allowing major Chinese banks to protect themselves from the consequences.
It has followed the same pattern since Operation Economic Outcast expanded secondary sanctions in August, criticising the measures without imposing another Iran-related countermeasure.

The calculation could change if the US sanctioned a major Chinese bank or state-owned enterprise rather than another shell company, small bank, or teapot refiner. China’s largest financial institutions depend heavily on access to dollars.
The US has far less leverage over smaller and less systemically important firms. This asymmetry makes an escalating spiral of US sanctions and Chinese countermeasures less likely.

The problem for the Trump administration is what happens as more transactions move beyond the institutions and payment channels most exposed to US pressure. At that point, effective enforcement increasingly requires cooperation from Chinese banks over which the US government has no authority.
A growing renminbi-based financial system does not make US sanctions ineffective, at least while major Chinese banks remain dependent on the global dollar-based system.

But when non-dollar payments are routed through shadow intermediaries, they erode the two critical enforcement advantages on which US financial sanctions have traditionally relied: the visibility of transactions and leverage over the institutions that process them.

While the dollar system gives the US enormous financial power, American officials can no longer assume that the threat of being excluded from it will be enough to make foreign institutions comply with their dictates.
As more of the actual enforcement takes place inside China’s domestic financial system, beyond the reach of American authorities, China may gain a new source of geopolitical leverage.
Expecting China to enforce US sanctions is unrealistic, but anti-money laundering enforcement offers a more practical basis for cooperation.

As US and Chinese officials discussed Iran and its financial ties to China ahead of Trump’s planned summit with Chinese president Xi Jinping in Washington, the US would have better luck pressing China to enforce its own anti-money laundering rules against the opaque financial networks facilitating Iranian trade.

Zongyuan Zoe Liu, senior fellow for China studies at the Council on Foreign Relations, is adjunct professor of international and public affairs at Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs.

cfbb66ce63407d51: In 2027, high-stakes national elections will be held in nine countries—France, Italy, Spain, Poland, Greece, Finland, Estonia, Slovakia, and Slovenia—that together account for over half of the European Union’s population.

Although these contests, as well as an indirect federal presidential election in Germany, will hinge on issues such as cost-of-living pressures, immigration, public debt, security, and social protections, a more fundamental question will run through them all: Do we Europeans want to remain masters of our own destiny, or will we allow the decisions that matter most to be made elsewhere?

The urgency of this choice is already apparent. The Alternative for Germany’s (AfD) recent victory in Saxony-Anhalt is a warning not only for Germany, but for all of Europe. Controlling our own destiny requires that we can defend ourselves as the US scales back its commitments to allies.

It also means maintaining support for Ukraine; upholding democracy, the rule of law, and media pluralism; harnessing AI for the common good; securing our military, scientific, technological, energy, and industrial autonomy; and preserving our social and environmental model.
Although the ingredients of European power already exist, they have yet to be melded into an effective compound. We Europeans often discuss defense without defining the sovereignty it should protect.

We allude to competitiveness without adequately implementing the solutions already identified to address Europe’s strategic vulnerabilities, and without pursuing the policies needed to significantly and structurally raise Europe’s growth potential. We speak of reindustrialisation without deciding how to finance it. And we proclaim the importance of AI without offering a social vision for it.

Such muddling through will not do. Echoing the Strasbourg Declaration of Nov 27, 2025, Canadian prime minister Mark Carney accurately described the breakdown of the international order as a result of the growing use of energy, technology, finance, and supply chains as instruments of power and coercion.
This issue came into sharper focus in Strasbourg on Sept 16, when Carney attended European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen’s State of the Union address as a guest of honour.
Carney has urged middle powers to act together as great-power rivalries intensify, and his presence at the event puts this task squarely on the EU’s political calendar.
But Europe’s ambition must go further. Rather than settle for middle-power status, it must become a democratic superpower—powerful, sovereign, and non-imperial.
That is why we founded the Europa Power Initiative, whose goal is to bring coherence to Europe’s efforts to adapt to the geopolitical challenges it faces.
Europe must be careful neither to overestimate nor underestimate its strengths. Its powerlessness in some areas is real, but in others, it is merely presumed.

Europeans must reckon with how to transform a supranational polity into a democratic, sustainable, and responsible power capable of defending its own interests, preserving its citizens’ freedoms, and offering a vision grounded in shared rules, cooperation, and multilateralism.
Fortunately, our citizens are not demanding “more Europe” in the abstract. They want the EU to be more than a mere market with shared rules and procedures.

They want it to become a real power capable of protecting, investing, anticipating, deciding, and acting when national-level policymaking is no longer sufficient. The choice, then, is not between one’s country and “Europe”. It is between declining individually or exercising power together.

By transforming the EU into a democratic power capable of acting swiftly in a crisis, we would be creating not a superstate that erases nations, but rather a community that enables states to exercise powers that none can wield alone.

Such a project would respect the will of Europe’s peoples and the diversity of its member states. It would establish common capabilities in decisive areas—defense, energy, research, semiconductors, cloud computing, data, AI, and investment—while keeping decision-making at the local or national level whenever that is most effective and legitimate (the subsidiarity principle).
True power does have a price; but continued powerlessness would cost more: deeper dependencies, weaker democracies, and the undermining of our social and environmental model and cohesion.

The key challenge is to avoid impossible choices like spending more on defense at the expense of health, education, research, social protection, climate action, or culture. Pooling investments that require scale, for example, could overcome this dilemma by increasing the impact of every euro spent.
Technological sovereignty is not merely about limiting the risks of AI. It also calls for harnessing new tools to improve healthcare, education, research, and governance.
It requires shared digital infrastructure controlled in Europe, measures to protect our citizens’ and businesses’ data, and expanded rights and freedoms to give everyone greater agency.

The 2027 elections will be national in form but European in consequence. Any decision by one state on defense, energy, immigration, industrialisation, Ukraine, or technology affects the others. Every European therefore has a stake in elections where they will not vote.

Managing this asymmetry demands better coordination among national campaigns: candidates should be asked similar questions, and the implications of their proposals for the EU should be compared. The point is not to erode European voters’ sovereignty, but to ensure that they are exercising it with full awareness of their interdependence.

Independent, diverse, innovative, and high-quality media—especially public-service media—have an essential role to play here. Joint investigations and transnational debates would give next year’s elections a European perspective, thereby cultivating a sense of shared consciousness.

The Europa Power Initiative was founded in Strasbourg in this spirit. With the goal of turning our interdependence into democratic debate and common proposals, our Oct 21–23 conference will bring together political leaders, experts, media representatives, and citizens to prepare for challenges Europe must confront.
Building the power to exercise sovereignty and preserve Europeans’ way of life means restoring our freedom to act together. There is no other way citizens can gain control over their future.

Guillaume Klossa is a former AI special adviser to the president of the European Commission and co-chair of the Europa Power Initiative. Catherine Trautmann, a former French minister of culture and communication, is mayor of Strasbourg, president of the Strasbourg Eurometropolis, and a co-founder of the Europa Power Initiative. Slavoj Žižek, professor of philosophy at the European Graduate School, is co-chair of the Europa Power Initiative.
